value.overview: The Rock Pigeon is a familiar, adaptable pigeon associated with people in towns and cities worldwide. It was originally native to rocky cliffs and caves across parts of Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, but domestic birds have been transported widely. Many free-flying populations are descended from domesticated stock and show highly variable plumage. In Costa Rica, it is mainly encountered as an introduced or feral urban bird rather than as a native forest species.
value.classification: The Rock Pigeon belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. Its scientific name is Columba livia. The names Rock Dove, Common Pigeon, and Feral Pigeon are also used, depending on regional or population context.
value.identification: A typical Rock Pigeon is a medium-sized, compact bird with a small head, short neck, broad pointed wings, and a longish tail. The common gray form has a pale gray body, darker head, iridescent green and purple on the neck, two black wing bars, a white rump, and a dark tail band. Plumage varies greatly, including white, black, brown, reddish, and mottled forms because of domestication and selective breeding. The bill is dark with a pale cere, and the legs are pinkish-red.
value.rangeHabitat: The species is native to rocky regions of Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, but feral populations now occur in many parts of the world. In Costa Rica, Rock Pigeons are introduced, human-associated birds found chiefly in cities, towns, agricultural settlements, transport centers, and other built-up areas. They commonly nest on building ledges, bridges, roofs, and other structures that resemble cliffs. They are generally uncommon in undisturbed forest and remote natural habitats.
value.migrationStatus: Rock Pigeons in Costa Rica are generally resident rather than migratory. Local movements may occur between feeding and roosting sites, but there is no regular long-distance migration associated with the introduced urban populations.
value.breeding: Rock Pigeons can breed throughout much of the year where food, water, and suitable nesting sites are available. They usually form simple nests of twigs, grass, and other debris on sheltered ledges or building structures. A typical clutch contains two white eggs, and both adults incubate them and feed the young with a nutritious crop secretion. Several broods may be produced annually under favorable urban conditions. Nesting behavior in Costa Rica is expected to be similar to that of other established feral populations.
value.dietFeeding: The Rock Pigeon mainly eats seeds, grains, and other plant material, but urban birds also consume food scraps and discarded human foods. It usually feeds on the ground in groups, walking and pecking in open areas, streets, plazas, farms, and around buildings. It drinks by placing its bill in water and drawing water continuously, an unusual method among birds. Dependence on human food can support very large concentrations in cities.
value.behavior: Rock Pigeons are social and often gather in flocks, especially around reliable food, water, roosting, and nesting sites. They spend much of the day feeding on the ground, resting on ledges, or flying between buildings. Their flight is rapid and direct, with frequent wingbeats and occasional gliding. Courtship includes cooing, head-bobbing, bowing, and short display flights. They commonly roost communally and may repeatedly use the same structures.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally stable at the global level, although local populations may increase or decrease in response to food availability, urban management, disease, and changes in buildings or nesting sites.
